blocks.text:
Design a Hotel Management System that lets guests book a room for a specific date range. The system must guarantee that a room is never booked for two overlapping stays, while correctly allowing one guest to check in on the exact day another checks out.

  • Actors: guests requesting a room for a specific check-in and check-out date.
  • Scope: a hotel with a fixed room inventory across multiple room types, date-range-based availability.
  • Goal: guarantee no room is ever double-booked for overlapping nights, while correctly allowing back-to-back stays.

The one rule this entire system exists to enforce: a room can never have two reservations whose date ranges genuinely overlap, but a checkout day and the next check-in day on the very same date is perfectly valid. Getting that boundary exactly right is the whole problem.

items: The system shall let a guest request a specific room for a specific check-in and check-out date.
The system shall reject a booking if the requested date range overlaps any existing reservation for that room.
The system shall allow a new reservation to check in on the exact day an existing reservation checks out.
The system shall calculate the total price based on the room’s type and the number of nights booked.
The system shall notify listeners of every booking outcome, confirmed or rejected.

metadata.alt: Four non-functional priorities: no overlap, correctness at boundaries, extensibility and observability

items: No overlap: a room must never carry two reservations that genuinely share even one night.
Correctness at boundaries: a checkout day and the next checkin day being the same date must be correctly treated as non-overlapping, not rejected.
Extensibility: new room types and new pricing rules (like seasonal rates) must be addable without rewriting the booking flow.
Observability: every booking outcome must be visible to anything watching the system.
Thread Safety: two guests requesting the same room with overlapping dates at nearly the same moment must never both succeed.
Should cancellation be supported, freeing up a room’s previously booked date range?
Do different room types need different cancellation policies or minimum stay lengths?
Should pricing support more than a fixed nightly rate, like weekend or seasonal pricing?
Is a single hotel enough, or do we need to support a chain with many properties?
Should the system support searching for any available room of a given type within a date range, not just checking one specific room id?
Dates are modeled as simple integer day numbers for this design, a real system would use an actual date type, the overlap logic itself is identical either way.
This design implements a fixed StandardRoomPricingStrategy, the pricing mechanism itself is pluggable for future strategies like seasonal pricing.
A checkout day and the next checkin day being identical is explicitly valid, matching standard hotel industry practice.
Cancellation is discussed as follow-up work, not implemented in the core flow shown here.
This design covers a single hotel’s room inventory, a real system would layer a Hotel/Chain hierarchy above it, discussed in Improvements.

metadata.alt: HotelReservationService composing Rooms, Reservations, a RoomPricingStrategy, and notifying ReservationObservers

items: Room: one physical room, identified by id, with a fixed type.
Reservation: one confirmed stay, its room, guest, and date range.
RoomPricingStrategy: however a room type’s nightly rate gets decided.
ReservationObserver: anything that wants to react to a booking succeeding or failing.
HotelReservationService: the orchestrator running the overlap-check-and-book flow.

metadata.alt: HotelReservationService managing a Room, which has multiple non-overlapping Reservations over time

items: Association: HotelReservationService is associated with every Room and every Reservation, neither owns the other’s lifecycle directly.
Association: a Reservation references its Room by id, allowing many reservations to exist for the same room across different, non-overlapping date ranges.
Association: HotelReservationService is associated with a RoomPricingStrategy and zero or more ReservationObservers, both swappable independently.
Realization: StandardRoomPricingStrategy realizes RoomPricingStrategy; ConsoleReservationObserver realizes ReservationObserver.

metadata.alt: HotelReservationService tying together Room, Reservation, RoomPricingStrategy and ReservationObserver

blocks.text: Notice that Reservation itself has no overlap-checking logic at all, that entire responsibility lives in HotelReservationService.isRoomAvailable(). This keeps Reservation a simple, predictable data holder.
Three patterns keep this design correct and genuinely extensible.

metadata.alt: RoomPricingStrategy as the shared contract behind a fixed-rate strategy and a future seasonal strategy

blocks.text: Why needed: nightly rates vary by room type today, and may need to vary by season or demand tomorrow. Why best: HotelReservationService only ever calls pricingStrategy.getPricePerNight(type), it never hardcodes a rate itself. What it solves: lets pricing evolve independently of the booking and overlap-checking logic.

metadata.alt: HotelReservationService notifying every registered ReservationObserver of both confirmations and rejections

blocks.text: Why needed: a real system needs to send confirmation emails and update a front-desk dashboard, all reacting to the same booking outcome. Why best: new observer types can be added freely with zero changes to the booking flow itself. What it solves: keeps notification concerns fully decoupled from the reservation logic.

metadata.alt: RoomFactory generating a full room inventory from just three counts

blocks.text: Why needed: manually constructing every Room object for a large hotel by hand would be repetitive and error-prone. Why best: RoomFactory centralizes exactly how room ids and types are generated, in one tested place. What it solves: makes building a hotel’s room inventory a single, reliable method call.

items: Room: responsibility is holding an id and a type. Attributes: id, type. Methods: getId(), getType().
Reservation: responsibility is holding one confirmed stay’s details. Attributes: id, roomId, guestName, checkInDay, checkOutDay.

HotelReservationService: responsibility is running the entire overlap-check-and-book workflow. Attributes: rooms, reservations, pricingStrategy, observers, reservationCounter. Methods: isRoomAvailable(), bookRoom(), addObserver().

metadata.alt: RoomPricingStrategy and ReservationObserver as the two extension points, each with one concrete implementation shown

blocks.text: RoomPricingStrategy isolates how a nightly rate is calculated. ReservationObserver isolates reactions to booking outcomes, letting any number of independent systems watch the same reservation service.
Three workflows matter most: a successful booking, a rejected overlapping booking, and the tricky back-to-back boundary case.

metadata.alt: A booking request checked against every existing reservation for the room, finding no overlap, and confirming

blocks.text: The overlap check runs against every existing reservation for that specific room before anything is ever created.

metadata.alt: A booking request rejected because its date range genuinely overlaps an existing reservation

blocks.text: The rejection happens before any reservation object is created, the room’s existing bookings are left completely untouched.

metadata.alt: A new booking starting on the exact day an existing reservation ends, correctly treated as non-overlapping

blocks.text: This is the case that separates a correct implementation from a subtly broken one, checkIn equal to an existing checkOut must NOT be treated as an overlap, the strict less-than comparisons in the overlap formula are exactly what make this work.

metadata.alt: The full booking sequence: validate the date range, check for overlap, then confirm or reject

items: Happy path: the date range is valid and does not overlap any existing reservation, the booking is confirmed with a correctly calculated price.
Failure, invalid range: checkIn is not strictly before checkOut, the booking is rejected immediately without ever touching the reservation list.
Failure, overlap: the requested range genuinely overlaps an existing reservation for that room, the booking is rejected with no state change.
Edge success, back-to-back: the requested checkIn exactly equals an existing reservation’s checkOut, correctly allowed.
HotelReservationService.bookRoom(roomId, guestName, checkIn, checkOut): the single entry point for attempting a booking.
HotelReservationService.isRoomAvailable(roomId, checkIn, checkOut): the core overlap check every booking decision is built on.
HotelReservationService.addObserver(ReservationObserver): registers a new observer for booking outcomes.
RoomFactory.createRooms(singleCount, doubleCount, suiteCount): the only way room inventories are built in this design.

metadata.alt: A booking request with checkIn on or after checkOut being rejected before any overlap check runs

items: Invalid input: a checkIn day on or after the checkOut day is rejected immediately, before any overlap logic is even attempted.
Resource unavailable: a room id that does not exist in the hotel’s inventory is rejected the same way as an overlapping request.
Business-rule violation: the overlap check is the single source of truth for availability, there is no code path that can create two genuinely overlapping reservations for the same room.
System failure: a broken reservation observer throwing an exception should be caught per-listener, never allowed to prevent a valid booking from actually confirming.

metadata.alt: Two guests requesting overlapping dates on the same room, guarded by a lock around the entire check-and-book sequence

blocks.text: bookRoom() reads the full reservation list during the overlap check, then writes a new reservation, as two separate steps. If two requests for overlapping dates on the same room run concurrently, both could pass the overlap check before either inserts. The entire check-and-insert sequence must be synchronized, ideally scoped per room (a lock per room id) rather than one global lock, so bookings for different rooms are never needlessly serialized against each other.

items: Adding seasonal pricing (higher rates during peak dates) requires only a new RoomPricingStrategy implementation, zero changes to the booking flow.
Adding an EmailConfirmationObserver that sends a real confirmation email is a pure ReservationObserver implementation.
Supporting cancellation would add a cancelReservation() method that removes a Reservation from the list, the existing isRoomAvailable() logic needs no changes at all.
Future work: searching for "any available room of type DOUBLE for these dates" would layer a new query method on top of isRoomAvailable(), reusing it directly rather than duplicating overlap logic.
Single Responsibility: Room only holds identity and type, Reservation only holds stay details, HotelReservationService only orchestrates the booking workflow.
Open/Closed: new pricing strategies and observer types can be added without modifying the existing, already-correct overlap-checking logic.
Liskov Substitution: any RoomPricingStrategy or ReservationObserver implementation can be substituted freely without HotelReservationService needing to know which one it has.
Interface Segregation: RoomPricingStrategy exposes exactly one method, ReservationObserver exposes exactly the two events it genuinely needs.
Dependency Inversion: HotelReservationService depends on the RoomPricingStrategy and ReservationObserver abstractions, never on a specific concrete implementation.
A one-night stay (checkOut equals checkIn plus one): correctly priced for exactly one night, not zero.
Two back-to-back reservations meeting at the exact same day: both must be allowed, this is the core boundary case the overlap formula is specifically designed to get right.
A room with zero existing reservations: the very first booking request for it always succeeds, since the overlap loop simply finds nothing to compare against.
A reservation request spanning many existing reservations at once (a very long stay): the overlap check must catch a conflict with ANY of them, not just the first one found.
isRoomAvailable(): O(n) where n is the number of existing reservations for that specific room, each compared with a constant-time overlap check.
bookRoom(): O(n) overall, dominated entirely by the overlap check.
RoomFactory.createRooms(): O(singleCount plus doubleCount plus suiteCount), directly proportional to the inventory size.
Space: O(total rooms) for the room map, O(total reservations) for the reservation list.

metadata.alt: HOTEL containing ROOM rows, each with its own list of RESERVATION records over time

blocks.text: HOTEL stores the property itself, ROOM tracks every room’s type within that hotel, and RESERVATION records each confirmed stay with its exact date range and price, the same overlap-checking query this design implements in memory translates directly into a SQL range-overlap query against this schema.

items: How would you index reservations per room (e.g. sorted by checkInDay) to make the overlap check faster than a linear scan for a very busy room?
How would you extend this design to support searching across all rooms of a given type for available dates?
How would you implement cancellation and, if needed, partial refunds based on how close to check-in the cancellation happens?
How would you extend this design to a multi-property hotel chain, searching availability across many hotels at once?

items: Why does the overlap formula use strict less-than on both sides (checkIn < existingCheckOut AND existingCheckIn < checkOut) instead of less-than-or-equal? Because using less-than-or-equal would incorrectly reject a perfectly valid back-to-back stay where one guest’s checkout day equals the next guest’s checkin day.

Why is availability checked by scanning reservations rather than maintaining a per-day boolean calendar for each room? For a small number of reservations per room, a linear scan is simple and fast enough, a calendar approach trades simplicity for better performance on rooms with very high booking density, discussed in Improvements.

Why does bookRoom() validate the date range (checkIn strictly before checkOut) before ever running the overlap check? Because a nonsensical date range should be rejected on its own merits, independent of whether any existing reservations happen to exist.

An alternative could maintain a sorted list (or interval tree) of reservations per room, allowing an O(log n) overlap check instead of O(n), valuable at very large scale, unnecessary complexity for a hotel’s typical booking volume.

A simpler design could reject any booking touching a date already touched by another reservation (a less precise, coarser check), easier to implement, but would incorrectly reject valid back-to-back stays.
Using a real date/time library instead of plain integers would be necessary in production for handling time zones and calendar edge cases, the core overlap algorithm itself is identical either way.
Persist every room and reservation (already modeled in the ER diagram) so bookings survive a server restart.
Add a database-level constraint or index supporting efficient overlap queries directly in SQL, mirroring the in-memory overlap check.
Rate-limit booking attempts per user to prevent a single client from repeatedly probing availability across many rooms.
Expose a read-only availability search API separately from bookRoom(), so a UI can show open dates without risking accidental mutation.
